fixes.answer: The consequences can be severe. Chronic overwork frequently leads to stress, burnout and serious health problems, both physical and mental. It also strains personal relationships, as work encroaches on time with family and friends. Ironically, it often reduces long-term productivity too. Essentially, neglecting your personal life for work is [[self-defeating]], [[taking a heavy toll]] that eventually [[undermines]] everything.
fixes.why: 'toll' is part of the idiom; marked 'taking a heavy toll'

fixes.answer: A society where people are [[chronically]] overworked tends to suffer from higher rates of stress-related illness and weaker family and community bonds. When people have no time or energy left, civic and social life [[deteriorates]]. Conversely, a society that values balance tends to be healthier, happier and arguably more productive in the long run. So it is genuinely a matter of [[collective]] wellbeing.

I am hopeful, though not entirely certain. There is a growing cultural awareness of the importance of wellbeing, and flexible and remote working could, if managed well, improve balance considerably. Concepts like the four-day week are [[gaining traction]]. However, there is a risk that [[constant connectivity]] could make things worse. So improvement is possible, but it will require a [[deliberate cultural shift]] rather than happening automatically.
fixes.why: 'shift' and 'automatically' are plain; marked 'gaining traction', 'constant connectivity', 'deliberate cultural shift'

fixes.answer: On a personal level, setting firm boundaries is crucial, such as not checking work emails after hours. Learning to prioritise and, importantly, to say no to excessive demands helps enormously. Making dedicated time for rest and relationships should be treated as [[non-negotiable]]. However, individuals can [[only do so much]]; employers must also foster a culture that genuinely respects personal time and does not reward [[overwork]].
fixes.why: 'respects' is plain; marked 'only do so much'

fixes.answer: The advantages are considerable: flexibility allows people to work when they are most productive and to fit work around personal commitments, which greatly improves balance. The disadvantage is that without a clear structure, work can [[bleed into]] all hours, and it requires strong [[self-discipline]]. It can also complicate team coordination. So flexibility is a wonderful benefit, provided it comes with sensible [[boundaries]] and mutual trust.

I respectfully disagree with framing it as either-or. Hard work is certainly important for achievement, and I value [[diligence]]. However, free time is not the opposite of hard work; it is what makes sustained hard work possible by preventing burnout. The two are [[complementary]]. In my view, someone who works intensely but never rests is not admirable but heading towards [[exhaustion]], so balance is wiser.
